![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/14b1144f52dcacc094901a159bf54c04f00daccc85df7b117b2163ed327dcd4f.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $2$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨x\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/614037b52ca1f60f03420019891af1004227e2e0f3b4a89d71adbdc68dadf1dd.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=2$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨x\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =2\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(y,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{D}r\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\pi \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(0,y,z)=⟨0\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
